title: Why Good Preparation Looks Like Nothing Happened
summary: Good prep shows up as a release nobody remembers. Why teams reward firefighting over prevention, how a premortem helps, and how to leave a trace of the work behind it.
author: Nguyen Le Phong
html:
Thursday night, a schema migration runs on production. Twelve minutes, no alerts, nobody gets paged. At standup the next morning someone says "smooth one, nice," and the team moves on to the next ticket.

What nobody saw: on Tuesday, the engineer who owned it ran the migration against a copy of production data. They wrote and tested a rollback script. They asked one annoying question ("how many old rows still have NULL in this column?") and found 3,000 of them from an import nobody remembered. Compare that with last month, when a different migration broke at 11 p.m. and someone stayed up until 2 a.m. fixing it. That person got a shout-out at the all-hands.

That's the odd thing about preparation. When it works, the result looks like nothing happened.

Nobody gets credit for problems that never happened

That line comes from an engineer at a car company, quoted by Nelson Repenning and John Sterman of MIT in a 2001 paper on why improvement programs keep failing (Nobody Ever Gets Credit for Fixing Problems that Never Happened). Their finding: organizations that lean on firefighting end up rewarding and promoting the people who save troubled projects with heroic last-minute effort, and they reward that "over the learning, training, and improvement activities that prevent such crises in the first place." One project leader told them plainly that delivering programs under duress was how he got where he is.

They also describe what they call the capability trap. Under pressure, people skip the preventive work, like maintenance, documentation or improvement meetings, to get today's output done. The cost doesn't show up right away, because capability takes time to wear down. So the shortcut looks free, and it becomes the habit. Teams then need more and more heroics just to stand still.

Swap "machine maintenance" for "dry run" or "runbook" and you'll recognize your own sprint. The preparation is the first thing cut, because skipping it costs nothing this week.

What preparation looks like on an ordinary day

Big moments obviously need prep: interviews, launches, a talk in front of the whole company. But most of it happens in small daily moves that nobody would think to praise:

  • Reading the code around a function before you change it, so you know who else calls it.
  • Opening the old customer complaint before you propose the "obvious" feature.
  • Writing down the real question before a 1:1, so it doesn't turn into twenty minutes of "so, how's it going?"
  • Putting in the PR description why the change is shaped this way and what you left out on purpose, so review starts from the decision and skips the guessing.

None of these makes you louder in a meeting. They make the meeting cheaper, because the obvious questions already have answers and the room can spend its time on the hard ones.

It often gets mistaken for slowness

Here's the awkward part. Someone says "let me check one dependency before I commit to Friday," and the room hears hesitation. Someone rewrites the release note so support can actually use it, and it looks like polishing. In the moment, preparation and dithering look alike. The difference only shows up later, when the Friday date holds.

A cheap way to make that pause feel legitimate is Gary Klein's premortem. After the team hears the plan, the lead asks everyone to imagine the plan has already failed, then each person writes down why (Klein, the Pre-mortem Method). Klein's point in his Harvard Business Review piece is that "too many people are reluctant to speak up about their reservations during the all-important planning phase." A premortem turns raising risks into the assignment. Doubting stops being a sign you're not a team player. Fifteen minutes, and the worried engineer's question about old NULL rows becomes a normal line on a list.

Preparation needs a question and a deadline

Preparation can also turn into a hiding place. Reading one more doc, tweaking one more slide, testing one more edge case nobody will hit. It feels responsible, and it keeps you from the part that feels exposed: shipping, speaking up, asking for the decision.

A simple test: can you name the question your prep answers, and when you'll stop? "Will this migration lock the orders table? I'll know after the dry run tomorrow" is preparation. "I want to feel more ready" is a mood, and moods don't have a done state. Useful prep makes the next step clearer. Once it does, take the step.

Make the invisible part a little visible

You don't need to brag about prep. You do need to leave a trace, because otherwise your team learns from the all-hands that only firefighting counts. A few low-key ways:

  • Add a "what I checked" section to PRs and release notes: "Dry run on prod snapshot, 12 min, rollback tested."
  • Keep the premortem list in the ticket, with what you did about each item.
  • If you lead a team, say it out loud in the retro: "Nothing broke Thursday because Lan ran a dry run and found 3,000 bad rows." That one sentence changes what people think gets rewarded.

Small repeated habits that pay off later are a topic of their own. If that's your kind of thing, this post on consistency picks it up from there.

Try this week

  • Before your next risky change, run a 15-minute premortem: "It's next Monday and this failed. Why?"
  • Give your prep a question and a stop time.
  • Add a "what I checked" line to one PR or release note.
  • Thank one teammate, by name, for a problem that didn't happen.

faqs.q: Why does preparation go unnoticed at work?
faqs.a: When preparation works, the result is that nothing goes wrong, and nobody celebrates a non-event. MIT researchers Repenning and Sterman found many organizations end up rewarding last-minute heroics over the prevention work that would have avoided the crisis.

A premortem is a short exercise from psychologist Gary Klein. After the team hears a plan, everyone imagines it has already failed and writes down why. It makes raising risks part of the job, so people share doubts they would otherwise keep to themselves.

faqs.q: How do I tell preparation from procrastination?
faqs.a: Preparation answers a specific question and has a stop point, like "Will this migration lock the orders table? I'll know after tomorrow's dry run." If you can't name the question or say when you'll stop, you're probably stalling.
